31976835.Title: A Novel Hydrocolloid Film Based on Pectin, Starch and Gunnera tinctoria and Ugni molinae Plant Extracts for Wound Dressing Applications

abstract.1: Background: The biodegradable and biocompatible nature of pectin-based films is of particular interest in wound dressing applications, due to its non-toxicity, pH-sensitivity and gelling activity.
abstract.2: An approach to improve the mechanical properties, the release profile of bioactive compounds as well as the performance in wet environments of pectin-based films is mixing with other biopolymers.
abstract.3: Objective: To prepare hydrocolloid films based on crosslinked pectin / starch blend loaded with bioactive extracts from leaves of G. tinctoria and U. molinae with controlled release of bioactive compounds and healing property.
abstract.4: Methods: The hydrocolloid films were characterized by FTIR, SEM, and TGA-FTIR techniques and their tensile properties, water uptake, and polyphenolic release profile in aqueous media were evaluated.
abstract.5: The dermal anti inflammatory activity of the hydrocolloid films was assessed by the mouse ear inflammation test.
abstract.6: The wound healing property of the loaded hydrocolloid films was explored in a rat model and in a clinical trial (sacrum pressure ulcer).
abstract.7: Results: The films showed an adequate water-uptake capacity between 100-160%.
abstract.8: The release of active compounds from the hydrocolloid films followed the Korsmeyer-Peppas equation.
abstract.9: The mechanical properties of hydrocolloid films were not affected by the plant extracts within the concentration range used.
abstract.10: The incorporation of the bioactive extracts in the polysaccharide films inhibited the topical edematous response by about 50%.
abstract.11: The topical application of the loaded hydrocolloid film on the pressure ulcer is completely closed after 17 days without showing any adverse reaction.
abstract.12: Conclusion: A novel hydrocolloid matrix was produced from crosslinked starch-pectin, which exhibited suitable chemical-physical properties to be used as a carrier of plant extracts with wound healing properties.

adaptation1.1: Pectin-based films are wrapping that is made from pectin, a substance extracted from ripe fruits. Pectin-based films are biodegradable and biocompatible. Additionally, the films are non-toxic, are pH (acid-base) sensitive, and have gelling activity. These qualities make the films of interest in wound dressing.
adaptation1.2: In order to improve how the films responsd to stress and strain, specifically how the material holds up when wet, other biopolymers could be mixed with the pectin-based films. Biopolymers are substances that are found within living organisms, just like pectin is found in fruit.
adaptation1.3: The aim of this study was the prepare hydrocolloid (gel-forming) films using a pectin and starch blend with extracts from two different leaves. The film was made to have a controlled release of bioactive compounds and healing properties. Bioactive compounds are components of food that influence biological or cellular activity within humans or animals that eat them.
adaptation1.4: The hydrocolloid films were tested for their tensile strength (resistance to tension breakage), water uptake, and polyphenolic release profile in wet environments. Polyphenols are compounds with various biological properties, including anti-inflammatory (anti-swelling and -redness from an infection) and antioxidant.
adaptation1.5: The skin anti-inflammatory activity of the hydrocolloid films was assessed (measured) by a test evaluating inflammation on a mouse ear.
adaptation1.6: The wound healing property of the hydrocolloid films was explored in a rat model. The wound healing property was also explored in a human clinical trial looking at lower back pressure ulcers (skin sores).
adaptation1.7: The films showed an adequate water-uptake capacity between 100-160%.
adaptation1.8: The release of active compounds from the hydrocolloid films followed the Korsmeyer-Peppas equation, which implies that release of healing properties was controlled over time.
adaptation1.9: The mechanical properties of the hydrocolloid films, or how they respond to stress, were not affected by the plant extracts.
adaptation1.10: Addition of the same bioactive extracts in a carbohydrate-based film significantly decreased the topical edematous response or the accumulation of watery fluid.
adaptation1.11: Applying the loaded hydrocolloid film on the pressure ulcer completely closed the wound after 17 days without any negative side effects.
adaptation1.12: The study concluded that a novel (new) hydrocolloid mixture was produced from starch and pectin. This mixture showed suitable chemical-physical properties to act as a carrier of plant extracts with wound healing properties.

adaptation2.1: The recycability of pectin-based films (thin strips of plant-based fiber) is of interest in wound bandaging, due to its non-toxicity, acid-sensitivity, and gel-like nature.
adaptation2.2: One idea to improve the function, bioactive composition, and performance when wet of pectin-based films is mixing it with other biological molecules.
adaptation2.3: Our objective is to create waterproof films based on a pectin/starch blend with specific plant extracts that have controlled release of bioactive and healing substances.
adaptation2.4: The molecular composition of the waterproof films were measured with specific tools. We also measured the tension strength, water uptake, and bioactive molecules released in water.
adaptation2.5: The skin-related anti-inflammatory activity of the waterproof films was measured by testing its anti-inflammatory eactivity on an inflammed mouse ear.
adaptation2.6: We tested the healing effects of the active waterproof films with rats and human bedsores.
adaptation2.7: The films showed an acceptable water-uptake capacity between 100-160%.
adaptation2.8: The release of biological compounds from the waterproof films followed a standard drug-release trend.
adaptation2.9: The function of the waterproof films was not affected by the plant extracts within the amounts used.
adaptation2.10: Adding plant extracts into the films blocked the skin swelling by around 50%.
adaptation2.11: The application of the active waterproof film on the surface of the bedsore is closed after 17 days without any side effects.
adaptation2.12: A new waterproof film was created from a starch-pectin blend, with suitable chemical-physical properties to carry plant extracts with wound healing effects.

34125728.Title: Medical Device-Related Pressure Injury to the Ear from a Mask

abstract.1: Mask wearing is now ubiquitous because of the COVID-19 pandemic and has given rise to medical device-related pressure injuries in persons at risk of skin breakdown.
abstract.2: The ear has unique anatomy that is particularly susceptible to injury from pressure.
abstract.3: In this time of mandatory personal protective equipment requirements in healthcare facilities, protection and assessment of skin in the vulnerable postauricular area are needed.
abstract.4: This article presents a case report of a pressure injury on the ear, reviews the anatomy of the ear, and provides strategies for assessment and treatment of pressure injuries in this often overlooked anatomic region.
abstract.5: Treating Mask-Related Pressure Injury: Begin by removing the offending device.
abstract.6: If the patient continues to require a mask, provide a mask or “ear saver” mask strap that secures around the head or back of the neck rather than the ear, although again, this does not remove the need for continued skin assessment to areas subjected to pressure and friction.
abstract.7: Infection should be considered and ruled out.
abstract.8: Local cellulitis is characterized by warmth, redness, pain, and swelling.
abstract.9: Presence of purulent discharge might indicate deeper infection and/or abscess.
abstract.10: If infection is present, treatment should be initiated with topical and/or systemic antibiotics, depending on culture and severity.
abstract.11: Removing hair in the area may be helpful, because it eliminates foreign body intrusion into the wound base, as well as a source of contamination, consistent with the principles of wound bed preparation.
abstract.12: It is important to note that a healed wound may not have the same physical strength as normal tissue and may be prone to recurrence, also known as recidivism.

adaptation1.1: Mark wearing is now present everywhere. This is because of the COVID-19 pandemic (a global, viral, respiratory illness). Mask wearing has increased medical device-related pressure injuries, or skin sores, in persons that have higher chances of their skin breaking down.
adaptation1.2: The ear has a unique structure that is more vulnerable to injury from pressure.
adaptation1.3: Right now is a time of mandatory personal protective equipment requirements in healthcare facilities. Continual wear of personal protective equipment requires care for and assessment (evaluation) of the skin of the ear.
adaptation1.4: This study presents a case of a pressure injury on the ear. This study will also review the anatomy of the ear and provide strategies for assessment and treatment of pressure injuries of the ear.
adaptation1.5: When treating a mask-related pressure injury, you first begin by removing the mask.
adaptation1.6: If the patient continues to require a mask, provide a mask or “ear saver” mask strap that secures around the head or back of the neck rather than the ear. However, providing an "ear saver" does not remove the need for continued monitoring of the skin areas that undergo continued pressure.
adaptation1.7: Infection should be considered and ruled out.
adaptation1.8: Local cellulitis (bacterial skin infection) is characterized by warmth, redness, pain, and swelling.
adaptation1.9: Presence of pus might indicate a deeper infection and/or abscess (swollen area with pus).
adaptation1.10: If there is signs of infection, treatment should be initiated with topical treatment (applied directly to the skin) and/or systemic antibiotics (drugs that affect the whole body). Treatment method chosen will depend on the skin health and severity of infection.
adaptation1.11: Removing hair in the area may be helpful. This may be helpful as it eliminates things that may stray into the wound. Additionally, hair is a source of contamination.
adaptation1.12: It is important to understand that a healed wound may not have the same physical strength as normal tissue. Additionally, healed skin may be vulnerable to reoccurring injuries, also known as recidivism.

abstract.1: Pressure injury (PI) corresponds to a skin damage of ischemic aetiology that affects the integrity of the skin and is produced by prolonged pressure or friction between a hard internal and external surface.

abstract.3: The use of autologous platelet-rich plasma (APRP) gel arises as a therapeutic possibility in the presence of chronic pressure injuries.
abstract.4: The case of a patient with chronic PI who has been treated with APRP is presented, achieving resolution of the lesion.

abstract.1: This review addresses the pathophysiology and treatment of hemorrhagic shock - a condition produced by rapid and significant loss of intravascular volume, which may lead sequentially to hemodynamic instability, decreases in oxygen delivery, decreased tissue perfusion, cellular hypoxia, organ damage, and death.
abstract.2: Hemorrhagic shock can be rapidly fatal.
abstract.3: The primary goals are to stop the bleeding and to restore circulating blood volume.
abstract.4: Resuscitation may well depend on the estimated severity of hemorrhage.
abstract.5: It now appears that patients with moderate hypotension from bleeding may benefit by delaying massive fluid resuscitation until they reach a definitive care facility.
abstract.6: On the other hand, the use of intravenous fluids, crystalloids or colloids, and blood products can be life saving in those patients who are in severe hemorrhagic shock.
abstract.7: The optimal method of resuscitation has not been clearly established.
abstract.8: A hemoglobin level of 7-8 g/dl appears to be an appropriate threshold for transfusion in critically ill patients with no evidence of tissue hypoxia.
abstract.9: However, maintaining a higher hemoglobin level of 10 g/dl is a reasonable goal in actively bleeding patients, the elderly, or individuals who are at risk for myocardial infarction.
abstract.10: Moreover, hemoglobin concentration should not be the only therapeutic guide in actively bleeding patients.
abstract.11: Instead, therapy should be aimed at restoring intravascular volume and adequate hemodynamic parameters.

25284231.Title: The ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic shock: a well established teaching tool on the edge?

abstract.1: Uncontrolled bleeding is the leading cause of shock in trauma patients and delays in recognition and treatment have been linked to adverse outcomes.
abstract.2: For prompt detection and management of hypovolaemic shock, ATLS(®) suggests four shock classes based upon vital signs and an estimated blood loss in percent.
abstract.3: Although this classification has been widely implemented over the past decades, there is still no clear prospective evidence to fully support this classification.
abstract.4: In contrast, it has recently been shown that this classification may be associated with substantial deficits.
abstract.5: A retrospective analysis of data derived from the TraumaRegister DGU(®) indicated that only 9.3% of all trauma patients could be allocated into one of the ATLS(®) shock classes when a combination of the three vital signs heart rate, systolic blood pressure and Glasgow Coma Scale was assessed.
abstract.6: Consequently, more than 90% of all trauma patients could not be classified according to the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic shock.
abstract.7: Further analyses including also data from the UK-based TARN registry suggested that ATLS(®) may overestimate the degree of tachycardia associated with hypotension and underestimate mental disability in the presence of hypovolaemic shock.
abstract.8: This finding was independent from pre-hospital treatment as well as from the presence or absence of a severe traumatic brain injury.
abstract.9: Interestingly, even the underlying trauma mechanism (blunt or penetrating) had no influence on the number of patients who could be allocated adequately.
abstract.10: Considering these potential deficits associated with the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic shock, an online survey among 383 European ATLS(®) course instructors and directors was performed to assess the actual appreciation and confidence in this tool during daily clinical trauma care.
abstract.11: Interestingly, less than half (48%) of all respondents declared that they would assess a potential circulatory depletion within the primary survey according to the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic shock.
abstract.12: Based on these observations, a critical reappraisal of the current ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic seems warranted.

adaptation1.2: For quick detection and management of hypovolemic shock, ATLS(®) suggests four shock classes. These classes are based upon vital signs and an estimated blood loss in percent. Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss with blood vessels or blood vascular system.
adaptation1.3: Although this classification has been widely used, there is no clear evidence to fully support this classification.
adaptation1.4: In contrast, it has recently been shown that this classification may be associated with substantial deficits.
adaptation1.5: Evaluation of data derived from the TraumaRegister DGU(®) indicated only 9.3% of all trauma patients could be placed into one of the ATLS(®) shock classes when a combination of the three vital signs was assessed (measured).
adaptation1.6: Because of this, more than 90% of all trauma patients could not be classified according to the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolemic shock.
adaptation1.7: Further review included data from the UK-based TARN registry. This evaluation suggested that ATLS(®) may overestimate the degree of tachycardia (high heart rate) associated with low blood pressure and underestimate mental disability in the presence of hypovolemic shock.
adaptation1.8: This finding was independent from pre-hospital treatment and from the presence or absence of a severe traumatic brain injury.
adaptation1.9: The underlying trauma mechanism, or what caused the injury, had no influence on the number of patients who could be categorized.
adaptation1.10: Considering these potential gaps associated with the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolemic shock, an online survey was conducted. The survey assessed 383 European ATLS(®) course instructors and directors. The survey was completed to assess the understanding and confidence in this tool during daily clinical trauma care.
adaptation1.11: Less than half of all respondents declared that they would assess a potential circulatory depletion within the primary survey according to the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolemic shock.
adaptation1.12: Based on these observations, a critical reappraisal (revision) of the current ATLS(®) classification of hypovolemic is needed.

25565640.Title: Individual-Specific, Beat-to-beat Trending of Significant Human Blood Loss: The Compensatory Reserve

abstract.1: Current monitoring technologies are unable to detect early, compensatory changes that are associated with significant blood loss.
abstract.2: We previously introduced a novel algorithm to calculate the Compensatory Reserve Index (CRI) based on the analysis of arterial waveform features obtained from photoplethysmogram recordings.
abstract.3: In the present study, we hypothesized that the CRI would provide greater sensitivity and specificity to detect blood loss compared with traditional vital signs and other hemodynamic measures.
abstract.4: Continuous noninvasive vital sign waveform data, including CRI, photoplethysmogram, heart rate, blood pressures, SpO2, cardiac output, and stroke volume, were analyzed from 20 subjects before, during, and after an average controlled voluntary hemorrhage of ∼1.2 L of blood.
abstract.5: Compensatory Reserve Index decreased by 33% in a linear fashion across progressive blood volume loss, with no clinically significant alterations in vital signs.
abstract.6: The receiver operating characteristic area under the curve for the CRI was 0.90, with a sensitivity of 0.80 and specificity of 0.76.
abstract.7: In comparison, blood pressures, heart rate, SpO2, cardiac output, and stroke volume had significantly lower receiver operating characteristic area under the curve values and specificities for detecting the same volume of blood loss.
abstract.8: Consistent with our hypothesis, CRI detected blood loss and restoration with significantly greater specificity than did other traditional physiologic measures.
abstract.9: Single measurement of CRI may enable more accurate triage, whereas CRI monitoring may allow for earlier detection of casualty deterioration.

adaptation1.1: Current monitoring technologies are unable to detect early changes associated with significant blood loss.
adaptation1.2: A novel model to calculate the Compensatory Reserve Index (CRI) was previously introduced by the authors in a secondary study. CRI measures physiological reserve, or how an organ responds to stress, which can be used as an indicator of how a patient will respond to intensive care.
adaptation1.3: In the present study, the authors hypothesized that the CRI would provide greater sensitivity and specificity to detect blood loss compared to traditional methods.
adaptation1.4: Vital signs were analyzed from 20 subjects before, during, and after an average controlled voluntary hemorrhage (excessive blood loss) of ∼1.2 L of blood.
adaptation1.5: CRI decreased across progressive blood volume loss, with no clinically significant alterations in vital signs.
adaptation1.6: Statistical analysis of CRI showed high confidence in the ability of the test to produce accurate results.
adaptation1.7: In contrast, blood pressures, heart rate, SpO2, cardiac output, and stroke volume had significantly lower confidence  for detection and specificity rates.
adaptation1.8: CRI detected blood loss and restoration with greater specificity than did other traditional measures.
adaptation1.9: Single measurement of CRI may enable more accurate assessment of health emergencies. CRI monitoring may allow for earlier detection of declining health.

adaptation2.1: Current monitoring technologies cannot detect early, counterbalancing changes associated with significant blood loss.
adaptation2.2: We previously showed a new mathematical equation to calculate the counterbalancing blood flow mechanics or Compensatory Reserve Index (CRI) based on analysis of blood vessel wave patterns from blood flow recordings.
adaptation2.3: In the present study, we theorized that CRI would give better accuracy to detect blood loss compared to standard vital signs and other blood flow measures.
adaptation2.4: We analyzed 20 subjects before, during, and after a regular, controlled voluntary blood loss of 1.2 liters for continuous non-surgical vital sign wave data, including CRI, recordings, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen levels, blood flow output, and blood volume.
adaptation2.5: CRI decreased by 33% in a linear trend across increasing blood volume loss, with no changes in vital signs.
adaptation2.6: CRI had high accuracy for detecting blood volume loss.
adaptation2.7: In comparison, blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen levels, blood flow output and blood volume had less accuracy for detecting the same amount of blood loss.
adaptation2.8: Consistent with out theory, CRI detected blood loss and restoration better than other traditional body measures.
adaptation2.9: Single measurement of CRI may enable better identification, while CRI monitoring may allow earlier detection of patient status trending towards death.

28346013.Title: The physiology of blood loss and shock: New insights from a human laboratory model of hemorrhage

abstract.1: Development of a human model of hemorrhage has provided a unique opportunity to investigate the underlying physiology that defines the individual capacity to avoid the life-threatening clinical condition of inadequate tissue oxygenation known as “shock.”
abstract.2: The experimental approach of progressively reducing central blood volume to the point of hemodynamic decompensation with the use of lower body negative pressure has revealed stark distinctions in the physiological compensatory responses between individuals with high compared with low tolerances to blood loss.
abstract.3: High tolerance to hemorrhage is defined by a capacity to maintain systemic perfusion pressure and reduce the rate of cerebral hypoperfusion by: (1) protecting cardiac output with greater elevations in heart rate associated with greater cardiac vagal withdrawal and sympathetically mediated adrenergic stimulation; (2) greater increases in systemic peripheral vascular resistance associated with higher sympathetic nerve activation and levels of circulating vasopressor endocrine responses; (3) alternating blood flow between the brain and peripheral tissue with greater sympathetically mediated oscillatory patterns of systemic pressure and flow; and (4) enhancing cardiac filling and cerebral perfusion pressure gradient by optimizing the respiratory pump.
abstract.4: When the capacity for these compensatory responses is exhausted, an active vasodilation drops resistance to blood flow allowing for increased perfusion of peripheral tissue.
abstract.5: When cardiac filling is no longer adequate to maintain systemic pressure and flow, a reflex-mediated pronounced bradycardia leads to the initiation of decompensatory shock.

adaptation1.1: A human model of hemorrhage (excessive bleeding) provides the opportunity to investigate the underlying mechanisms that can help someone avoid the life-threatening condition of inadequate tissue oxygenation known as "shock."
adaptation1.2: This is completed by experimentally reducing central blood volume. Blood volume is progressively decreased to the point of critically low blood pressure. This test approach has shown differences in the bodily responses between individuals with high tolerances versus low tolerances to blood loss.
adaptation1.3: High tolerance to hemorrhage is defined by maintaining body wide blood flow pressure and prevent decreased brain blood pressure. This is done by one of four ways.  First, by protecting cardiac output with greater elevations in heart rate associated with greater cardiac vagal withdrawal and sympathetically mediated adrenergic stimulation. Second, a greater increases in systemic peripheral vascular resistance (blood vessel resistance) associated with higher sympathetic nerve activation (fight-or-flight reaction) and levels of circulating vasopressor endocrine responses (responses from chemical messengers). Third, an alternating blood flow between the brain and peripheral tissue with greater sympathetically mediated oscillatory patterns of systemic pressure and flow. Lastly, by enhancing cardiac filling and cerebral perfusion pressure gradient (pressure driving oxygen to brain tissue) by optimizing the respiratory pump (muscles that help the lung extract and contract).
adaptation1.4: When these compensatory responses are exhausted, an active vasodilation (enlargement of blood vessels) drops resistance to blood flow allowing for increased perfusion of peripheral tissue.
adaptation1.5: When the body no is longer able to maintain systemic pressure and flow, a decreased heart rate leads to the initiation of decompensatory shock.

abstract.1: Etiology: Though most commonly thought of in the setting of trauma, there are numerous causes of hemorrhagic shock that span many systems.
abstract.2: Blunt or penetrating trauma is the most common cause, followed by upper and lower gastrointestinal sources.
abstract.3: Obstetrical, vascular, iatrogenic, and even urological sources have all been described.
abstract.4: Bleeding may be either external or internal.
abstract.5: A substantial amount of blood loss to the point of hemodynamic compromise may occur in the chest, abdomen, or retroperitoneum.
abstract.6: The thigh itself can hold up to 1 L to 2 L of blood.
abstract.7: Pathophysiology: Hemorrhagic shock is due to the depletion of intravascular volume through blood loss to the point of being unable to match the tissues demand for oxygen.
abstract.8: As a result, mitochondria are no longer able to sustain aerobic metabolism for the production of oxygen and switch to the less efficient anaerobic metabolism to meet the cellular demand for adenosine triphosphate.
abstract.9: In the latter process, pyruvate is produced and converted to lactic acid to regenerate nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to maintain some degree of cellular respiration in the absence of oxygen.
abstract.10: The body compensates for volume loss by increasing heart rate and contractility, followed by baroreceptor activation resulting in sympathetic nervous system activation and peripheral vasoconstriction.
abstract.11: Typically, there is a slight increase in the diastolic blood pressure with narrowing of the pulse pressure.
abstract.12: As diastolic ventricular filling continues to decline and cardiac output decreases, systolic blood pressure drops.
abstract.13: Due to sympathetic nervous system activation, blood is diverted away from noncritical organs and tissues to preserve blood supply to vital organs such as the heart and brain.
abstract.14: While prolonging heart and brain function, this also leads to other tissues being further deprived of oxygen causing more lactic acid production and worsening acidosis.
abstract.15: This worsening acidosis along with hypoxemia, if left uncorrected, eventually causes the loss of peripheral vasoconstriction, worsening hemodynamic compromise, and death.
abstract.16: The body’s compensation varies by cardiopulmonary comorbidities, age, and vasoactive medications.
abstract.17: Due to these factors, heart rate and blood pressure responses are extremely variable and, therefore, cannot be relied upon as the sole means of diagnosis.

adaptation1.1: Though most found in trauma cases, there are numerous causes of hemorrhagic (excessive bleeding) shock stemming from various organ systems.
adaptation1.2: Blunt or penetrating trauma (injury) is the most common cause. Additional causes include upper and lower gastrointestinal (stomach) sources.
adaptation1.3: Obstetrical (related to childbirth), vascular (related to blood vessels), iatrogenic (illness caused by medical exams), and even urological (related to the urinary tract) sources have all been described.
adaptation1.4: Bleeding may be either external or internal.
adaptation1.5: A substantial amount of blood loss, to the point of dysregulated (incorrect) blood flow, may occur in the chest, abdomen, or in the retroperitoneum. The retroperitoneum is area in the back of the abdomen not covered by the peritoneum.
adaptation1.6: The thigh can hold up to 1 L to 2 L of blood.
adaptation1.7: Hemorrhagic shock is caused by the blood loss in vessels to the point of being unable to match the tissues demand for oxygen.
adaptation1.8: As a result, mitochondria (cell part responsible for making chemical energy) are unable to sustain metabolisms needed for oxygen production. Mitochondria switch to the less efficient metabolism to meet cell demand.
adaptation1.9: Pyruvate, a chemical product of energy production, is produced and converted to maintain some cellular respiration (energy creation) in the absence of oxygen.
adaptation1.10: The body compensates for volume loss by increasing heart rate and contractions. These alterations are followed by baroreceptor activation, which is the increased activity of receptors to regulate blood pressure. The resulting endpoints are sympathetic nervous system activation (fight-or-flight activation) and constriction of blood vessels. The sympathetic nervous system is responsible for heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate, and pupil size.
adaptation1.11: There is normally a slight increase in the diastolic blood pressure (when the heart is relaxed) with decreased pulse pressure.
adaptation1.12: As the rate in which the heart fills with blood declines and cardiac output decreases, systolic blood pressure (heart is contracting) drops.
adaptation1.13: Due to sympathetic nervous system activation, blood is moved away from noncritical organs and tissues. This is done to preserve blood supply to vital organs like the heart and brain.
adaptation1.14: While prolonging heart and brain function, this blood movement leads to other tissues being deprived of oxygen. This deprivation can cause more lactic acid production and a build up of acid in the blood.
adaptation1.15: This acid build up along with low blood oxygen, if left uncorrected, eventually causes the loss of peripheral vasoconstriction (narrowed blood vessels), decreased blood flow, and death.
adaptation1.16: How the body handles this varies by accompanying heart and lung diseases, age, and blood pressure medications.
adaptation1.17: Due to these factors, heart rate and blood pressure responses are extremely different between patients. Therefore, heart rate and blood pressure cannot be the sole reasons of diagnosis.

29329171.Title: Nonhuman Primate (Rhesus Macaque) Models of Severe Pressure-Targeted Hemorrhagic and Polytraumatic Hemorrhagic Shock

abstract.1: Background: We endeavored to develop clinically translatable nonhuman primate (NHP) models of severe polytraumatic hemorrhagic shock.
abstract.2: Methods: NHPs were randomized into five severe pressure-targeted hemorrhagic shock (PTHS) ± additional injuries scenarios: 30-min PTHS (PTHS-30), 60-min PTHS (PTHS-60), PTHS-60 + soft tissue injury (PTHS-60+ST), PTHS-60+ ST + femur fracture (PTHS-60+ST+FF), and decompensated PTHS+ST+FF (PTHS-D).
abstract.3: Physiologic parameters were recorded and blood samples collected at five time points with animal observation through T = 24 h.
abstract.4: Results presented as mean ± SEM; statistics: log transformation followed by two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni multiple comparisons, Wilcoxon nonparametric test for comparisons, and the Friedmans' one-way ANOVA; significance: P < 0.05.
abstract.5: Results: Percent blood loss was 40% ± 2, 59% ± 3, 52% ± 3, 49% ± 2, and 54% ± 2 for PTHS-30, PTHS-60, PTHS-60+ST, PTHS-60+ST+FF, and PTHS-D, respectively.
abstract.6: All animals survived to T = 24 h except one in each of the PTHS-60 and PTHS-60+ST+FF groups and seven in the PTHS-D group.
abstract.7: Physiologic, coagulation, and inflammatory parameters demonstrated increasing derangements with increasing model severity.
abstract.8: Conclusion: NHPs exhibit a high degree of resilience to hemorrhagic shock and polytrauma as evidenced by moderate perturbations in metabolic, coagulation, and immunologic outcomes with up to 60 min of profound hypotension regardless of injury pattern.
abstract.9: Extending the duration of PTHS to the point of decompensation in combination with polytraumatic injury, evoked derangements consistent with those observed in severely injured trauma patients which would require ICU care.
abstract.10: Thus, we have successfully established a clinically translatable NHP trauma model for use in testing therapeutic interventions to trauma.

adaptation1.1: This study aimed to develop nonhuman primate (monkey) (NHP) models of severe polytraumatic (many-injury) hemorrhagic (excessive bleeding) shock that are applicable to human health settings.
adaptation1.2: NHPs were placed into five pressure-targeted hemorrhagic shock (PTHS) scenarios. The scenarios were as follows: 30-min PTHS (PTHS-30), 60-min PTHS (PTHS-60), PTHS-60 + soft tissue injury (PTHS-60+ST), PTHS-60+ ST + femur (leg) fracture (PTHS-60+ST+FF), and decompensated PTHS+ST+FF (PTHS-D).
adaptation1.3: Physiologic parameters were recorded. Blood samples were collected at five time points with animal observation through 24 hours.
adaptation1.5: Blood loss percentages were  40%, 59%, 52%, 49%, and 54% for PTHS-30, PTHS-60, PTHS-60+ST, PTHS-60+ST+FF, and PTHS-D, respectively.
adaptation1.6: All animals survived till the end of the study except one in the PTHS-60 and PTHS-60+ST+FF groups. Seven did not survive till the end of the study in the PTHS-D group.
adaptation1.7: Physiologic (overall health), coagulation (blood clotting), and inflammatory (infection-fighting) parameters showed increased disturbance with increasing model severity.
adaptation1.8: NHPs show a high degree of resilience to hemorrhagic shock and polytrauma (more than one injury). This was shown by moderate disturbances in metabolic, coagulation, and immunologic outcomes with low blood pressure in all injury groups.
adaptation1.9: Increasing PTHS duration to the point of organ failure with polytraumatic injury, evoked (led to) disturbances consistent with those observed in severely injured trauma patients requiring ICU care.
adaptation1.10: This study has successfully established a clinically translatable NHP trauma model for use in testing therapeutic interventions to trauma.

abstract.1: The term "shock" refers to a life-threatening circulatory failure caused by an imbalance between the supply and demand of cellular oxygen.
abstract.2: Hypovolemic shock is characterized by a reduction of intravascular volume and a subsequent reduction in preload.
abstract.3: The body compensates the loss of volume by increasing the stroke volume, heart frequency, oxygen extraction rate, and later by an increased concentration of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate with a rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve.
abstract.4: Hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock impairs the macrocirculation and microcirculation and therefore affects many organ systems (e.g. kidneys, endocrine system and endothelium).
abstract.5: For further identification of a state of shock caused by bleeding, vital functions, coagulation tests and hematopoietic procedures are implemented.
abstract.6: Every hospital should be in possession of a specific protocol for massive transfusions.
abstract.7: The differentiated systemic treatment of bleeding consists of maintenance of an adequate homeostasis and the administration of blood products and coagulation factors.

adaptation1.1: "Shock" refers to a life-threatening circulatory failure. Shock is caused by an imbalance between the supply and demand of oxygen within cells.
adaptation1.2: Hypovolemic shock is characterized by a decreased volume in blood vessels and a subsequent reduction in preload (volume of blood within the heart when its relaxed).
adaptation1.3: The body compensates the volume loss by increasing stroke volume, heart frequency, and oxygen extraction rate. Following these steps, the body will then increase 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (a chemical that controls oxygen movement) to increase available oxygen.
adaptation1.4: Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss with blood vessels or blood vascular system. Hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock impairs blood circulation. Because of this, this type of shock affects many organ systems.
adaptation1.5: Vital functions, coagulation (blood) tests, and hematopoietic (blood cell creation) procedures are used to identify a state of shock caused by bleeding.
adaptation1.6: Every hospital should have a specific protocol for massive transfusions (transfers).
adaptation1.7: Treatment of bleeding within the body consists of homeostasis (bodily equilibrium) maintenance and administration (use) of blood products and blood clothing (scabbing) medications.

adaptation2.1: The term "shock" refers to a life-threatening blood-flow-related failure caused by an imbalance between supply and demand of oxygen for cells.
adaptation2.2: Hypovolemic shock is due to a reduced amount of blood in vessels and subsequently reduced amount of blood and oxygen to pump.
adaptation2.3: The body compensates for the loss of volume by increasing blood volume per pump, heart rate, oxygen extraction rate, and increasing the amount of a specific molecule that increases oxygen release.
adaptation2.4: Hypovolemic shock from blood loss impairs blood circulation and affects many organs (e.g., kidneys, hormonal system, and blood vessel tubing).
adaptation2.5: For futher identification of shock due to bleeding, vital functions, blood clotting or thickening tests and procedures assessing blood cell development are used.
adaptation2.6: Every hospital should have a specific guideline for massive transfusions or transfers.
adaptation2.7: The personalized full-body treatment of bleeding includes maintaing a proper balance in the body and administering blood substances and factors for blood clotting.

30068251.Title: Unmasking the Hypovolemic Shock Continuum: The Compensatory Reserve

abstract.1: Hypovolemic shock exists as a spectrum, with its early stages characterized by subtle pathophysiologic tissue insults and its late stages defined by multi-system organ dysfunction.
abstract.2: The importance of timely detection of shock is well known, as early interventions improve mortality, while delays render these same interventions ineffective.
abstract.3: However, detection is limited by the monitors, parameters, and vital signs that are traditionally used in the intensive care unit (ICU).
abstract.4: Many parameters change minimally during the early stages, and when they finally become abnormal, hypovolemic shock has already occurred.
abstract.5: The compensatory reserve (CR) is a parameter that represents a new paradigm for assessing physiologic status, as it comprises the sum total of compensatory mechanisms that maintain adequate perfusion to vital organs during hypovolemia.
abstract.6: When these mechanisms are overwhelmed, hemodynamic instability and circulatory collapse will follow.
abstract.7: Previous studies involving CR measurements demonstrated their utility in detecting central blood volume loss before hemodynamic parameters and vital signs changed.
abstract.8: Measurements of the CR have also been used in clinical studies involving patients with traumatic injuries or bleeding, and the results from these studies have been promising.
abstract.9: Moreover, these measurements can be made at the bedside, and they provide a real-time assessment of hemodynamic stability.
abstract.10: Given the need for rapid diagnostics when treating critically ill patients, CR measurements would complement parameters that are currently being used.
abstract.11: Consequently, the purpose of this article is to introduce a conceptual framework where the CR represents a new approach to monitoring critically ill patients.
abstract.12: Within this framework, we present evidence to support the notion that the use of the CR could potentially improve the outcomes of ICU patients by alerting intensivists to impending hypovolemic shock before its onset.

adaptation1.1: Hypovolemic shock is a spectrum of reactions. In the early stages of hypovolemic shock, there is subtle pathophysiologic tissue insults. In the late stages of hypovolemic shock, there is multi-system organ dysfunction. Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss with blood vessels or blood vascular system.
adaptation1.2: Timely detection of shock is important. Early interventions (treatments) decrease the chance of death. Intervention delays can make the same interventions ineffective.
adaptation1.3: Detection can be limited by monitoring, parameters, and vital signs that are used in the intensive care unit (ICU).
adaptation1.4: Most parameters barely change during the early stages. When the signs finally become abnormal, hypovolemic shock has already occurred.
adaptation1.5: The compensatory reserve (CR) is a parameter. It is a new model for assessing body function. CR represents all of the mechanisms or ways the body compensates for internal conditions that dysregulate blood flow to vital organs during hypovolemia.
adaptation1.6: When these mechanisms are overwhelmed, unstable blood pressure, and circulatory failure will follow.
adaptation1.7: Previous studies involving CR measurements have shown its use in detecting central blood volume loss before blood pressure parameters and vital signs changed.
adaptation1.8: CR measurements have also been used in clinical studies involving patients with traumatic injuries or bleeding. The results from these clinical studies have been promising.
adaptation1.9: CR measurements can be made at the bedside. They also provide a real-time assessment of blood flow.
adaptation1.10: There is a need for rapid diagnostics when treating critically ill patients. CR measurements would complement parameters that are currently being used.
adaptation1.11: The aim of this article is to introduce a conceptual framework where the CR represents a new approach to monitoring critically ill patients.
adaptation1.12: Within this framework, the authors present evidence to support the how the use of the CR could potentially improve the outcomes of ICU patients. CR could improve alerting doctors to impending hypovolemic shock before its onset.

30573009.Title: The Nomenclature, Definition and Distinction of Types of Shock

abstract.1: Background: A severe mismatch between the supply and demand of oxygen is the common feature of all types of shock.
abstract.2: We present a newly developed, clinically oriented classification of the various types of shock and their therapeutic implications.
abstract.3: Results: There are only four major categories of shock, each of which is mainly related to one of four organ systems.
abstract.4: Hypovolemic shock relates to the blood and fluids compartment while distributive shock relates to the vascular system; cardiogenic shock arises from primary cardiac dysfunction; and obstructive shock arises from a blockage of the circulation.
abstract.5: Hypovolemic shock is due to intravascular volume loss and is treated by fluid replacement with balanced crystalloids.
abstract.6: Distributive shock, on the other hand, is a state of relative hypovolemia resulting from pathological redistribution of the absolute intravascular volume and is treated with a combination of vasoconstrictors and fluid replacement.
abstract.7: Cardiogenic shock is due to inadequate function of the heart, which shall be treated, depending on the situation, with drugs, surgery, or other interventional procedures.
abstract.8: In obstructive shock, hypoperfusion due to elevated resistance shall be treated with an immediate life-saving intervention.
abstract.9: Pathogenesis and pathophysiology: The characteristic feature of both, hemorrhagic and traumatic hemorrhagic shock is bleeding.
abstract.10: However, differences exist between the two subcategories in terms of the extent of soft tissue damage.
abstract.11: Clinically the most significant cause of hemorrhagic shock is acute bleeding from an isolated injury to a large blood vessel, gastrointestinal bleeding, nontraumatic vascular rupture (e.g., aortic aneurysm), obstetric hemorrhage (e.g., uterine atony), and hemorrhage in the region of the ear, nose, and throat (vascular erosion).
abstract.12: The shock is triggered by the critical drop in circulating blood volume; massive loss of red blood cells intensifies the tissue hypoxia.

adaptation1.1: Inequality between the supply and demand of oxygen is the common feature of shock.
adaptation1.2: This study presents a newly developed, patient-treatment oriented classification of the various types of shock and their therapeutic (helpful) implications.
adaptation1.3: There are four major categories of shock. Each category is mainly related to one of four organ systems.
adaptation1.4: One category, known as hypovolemic shock, relates to the blood and fluids compartment. Distributive shock relates to the vascular system or blood vessels. Cardiogenic shock arises from primary cardiac or heart dysfunction. Obstructive shock arises from a blockage of circulation.
adaptation1.5: Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss with blood vessels or blood vascular system. This type of shock is treated by replacement with balanced fluids.
adaptation1.6: Distributive shock is a state of low blood plasma. This type of shock comes from volume displacement in blood vessels. It is treated with a combination of vasoconstrictors, drugs that constrict blood vessels to increase blood pressure, and fluid replacement.
adaptation1.7: Cardiogenic shock is caused by inadequate function of the heart, which shall be treated, depending on the situation, with drugs, surgery, or other treatment methods.
adaptation1.8: In obstructive shock, circulatory failure due to increased resistance will be treated with an immediate life-saving intervention.
adaptation1.9: Both hemorrhagic (excessive bleeding from a ruptured blood vessel) and traumatic hemorrhagic (internal bleeding from an injury) shock feature bleeding.
adaptation1.10: However, differences exist between the two subcategories in terms of how much soft tissue damage they create.
adaptation1.11: The most significant cause of hemorrhagic shock is bleeding from an isolated injury to a critical portion of the body. Some of examples of this include injuries to blood vessels or blood within the intestines.
adaptation1.12: The shock is caused by a critical drop in circulating blood volume. Massive loss of red blood cells increases tissue hypoxia (below normal level of oxygen).

31030706.Title: Use of Shock Index to Identify Mild Hemorrhage: An Observational Study in Military Blood Donors

abstract.1: Introduction: Hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable death in combat, although early recognition of hemorrhage is still challenging on the battlefield.
abstract.2: Hypothesis/Problem: The objective of this study was to describe the shock index (SI) in a healthy military population, and to measure its variation during a controlled blood loss, simulated by blood donation.
abstract.3: Methods: A prospective observational study that enrolled military subjects, volunteers for blood donation, was conducted.
abstract.4: Demographic and clinical information, concerning both the patient and the blood collection, were recorded.
abstract.5: Baseline vital signs were measured, before and after donation, in a 45° supine position.
abstract.6: Statistical analysis was performed after calculation of SI.
abstract.7: Results: A total of 483 participants were included in the study.
abstract.8: The mean blood donation volume was 473mL (SD = 44mL).
abstract.9: The median pre- and post-blood donation SI were significantly different: 0.54 (IQR = 0.48-0.63) and 0.57 (IQR = 0.49-0.66), respectively (P = .002).
abstract.10: Changes in pre-/post-donation blood pressure (BP) and heart rate (HR) also reached statistical difference but represented a clinically poor relevance.
abstract.11: The multivariate analysis showed no significant associations between SI variations and age, sex, body mass index (BMI), sport activities, blood donation volume, and enteral volume replacement (EVR).
abstract.12: Conclusion: In this model of mild hemorrhage, SI exhibited significant variations but failed to reach clinical relevance.
abstract.13: Further studies are needed to prove the benefit of SI calculation as a possible parameter for early recognition of hemorrhage in combat casualties at the point of injury.

adaptation1.1: Hemorrhage (excessive bleeding) is the leading cause of preventable death in combat. However, early recognition of hemorrhage is still challenging on the battlefield.
adaptation1.2: The aim of this study was to describe the shock index (SI) in a healthy military population. Additionally, the paper aimed to measure SI variation during a controlled blood loss, simulated by blood donation.
adaptation1.3: A study that enrolled military subjects, volunteers for blood donation, was conducted.
adaptation1.4: Demographic (e.g. age, race) and clinical information, concerning both the patient and the blood collection, were recorded.
adaptation1.5: Vital signs were measured before and after donation.
adaptation1.6: Statistical analysis was performed after calculation of SI.
adaptation1.7: A total of 483 participants were included in the study.
adaptation1.8: The average blood donation volume was 473 mL.
adaptation1.9: The median (average) pre- and post-blood donation SI were significantly different.
adaptation1.10: Changes in pre-/post-donation blood pressure and heart rate were also different. However, the difference was of clinically poor relevance.
adaptation1.11: A statistical analysis showed no significant associations between SI variations and age, sex, body mass index (BMI), sport activities, blood donation volume, and enteral (intestinal) volume replacement (EVR).
adaptation1.12: The study concluding that SI exhibited significant variations (differences) but failed to reach clinical relevance.
adaptation1.13: Further studies are needed to prove the benefit of SI calculation as a possible method of early recognition of hemorrhage in combat casualties.

3146300.Title: A cluster of Pallister-Hall syndrome cases, (congenital hypothalamic hamartoblastoma syndrome)

abstract.1: We report on three infants with hand anomalies and congenital hypopituitarism.
abstract.2: In two of the cases, a hypothalamic tumor was found; the third infant died without postmortem brain studies.
abstract.3: Family history in the first case suggested possible familial recurrence; the mother's sister had died at 17 hr of age with polydactyly, microglossia, and flat nasal bridge (no autopsy done).
abstract.4: Our second case was born by cesarean section after a pregnancy complicated by extremely low maternal estriols.
abstract.5: At birth, hypopituitarism was diagnosed, a cranial CT scan was read as normal, and hormonal replacement was begun with thyroxine, hydrocortisone, and growth hormone.
abstract.6: At 11.5 mo of age she developed seizures; and a repeat CT scan showed a mass extending beneath the hypothalamus.
abstract.7: This tumor was removed surgically at 12 mo, the first successful treatment of this disorder.
abstract.8: Our third possible case had a bifid epiglottis, hypopituitarism, and hand anomalies.
abstract.9: A CT scan at birth failed to reveal a mass in the hypothalamus.
abstract.10: This child died from complications of untreated hypopituitarism, and no neuropathology studies were done.
abstract.11: These three cases were conceived between March 10th and April 17th in three different years in three geographically contiguous counties of Vermont.
abstract.12: Clustering in time and space and possible familial recurrence, in one of these cases, suggest a possible gene/environment interaction.

adaptation2.1: We report on three infants born with hands born with hand defects and defects of the pituitary gland, which regulates body functions and growth through chemical substances called hormones.
adaptation2.2: Two of the newborns had hypothalamic tumors (noncancerous growths in the base of their brains). The brain of the third newborn was not examined.
adaptation2.3: In one case, the disease runs in the family. The mother's sister died at the age of 17. She had extra fingers, extremely small tongue, and flat nose.
adaptation2.4: The mother of the second newborn had very low levels of estriol, a hormone made during pregnancy that is used to measure the unborn baby's health.
adaptation2.5: When this baby was born, brain imaging was normal, but the levels of hormones that regulate growth and development were low. Treatment with growth and other hormones was started.
adaptation2.6: At 11.5 months the baby started having seizures. A new brain imaging showed a mass in the lower part of the brain.
adaptation2.7: Surgery to remove this mass at 12 months was the first successful treatment of this disorder.
adaptation2.8: The third newborn had a split in the flap that protects the windpipe, lack of hormones that regulate growth and development, and abnormal hands.
adaptation2.9: Brain imaging at birth did not show a mass in the lower part of the brain.
adaptation2.10: This child died from complications of a brain mass that was not showing in the image.
adaptation2.11: These three babies were conceived between March 10th and April 17th in three different years in three neighboring counties of Vermont.
adaptation2.12: Close locations and possible other PHS cases in one of these families suggest inheritance and environment might interact.

9054938.Title: GLI3 frameshift mutations cause autosomal dominant Pallister-Hall syndrome

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS, M146510) was first described in 1980 in six newborns.
abstract.2: It is a pleiotropic disorder of human development that comprises hypothalamic hamartoma, central polydactyly, and other malformations.
abstract.3: This disorder is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait and has been mapped to 7p13 (S. Kang et al.Autosomal dominant Pallister-Hall syndrome maps to 7p13. Am. J. Hum. Genet. 59, A81 (1996)), co-localizing the PHS locus and the GLI3 zinc finger transcription factor gene.
abstract.4: Large deletions or translocations resulting in haploinsufficiency of the GLI3 gene have been associated with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome (GCPS; M175700) although no mutations have been identified in GCPS patients with normal karyotypes.
abstract.5: Both PHS and GCPS have polysyndactyly, abnormal craniofacial features and are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, but they are clinically distinct.
abstract.6: The polydactyly of GCPS is commonly preaxial and that of PHS is typically central or postaxial.
abstract.7: No reported cases of GCPS have hypothalamic hamartoma and PHS does not cause hypertelorism or broadening of the nasal root or forehead.
abstract.8: The co-localization of the loci for PHS and GCPS led us to investigate GLI3 as a candidate gene for PHS.
abstract.9: Herein we report two PHS families with frameshift mutations in GLI3 that are 3' of the zinc finger-encoding domains, including one family with a de novo mutation.
abstract.10: These data implicate mutations in GLI3 as the cause of autosomal dominant PHS, and suggest that frameshift mutations of the GLI3 transcription factor gene can alter the development of multiple organ systems in vertebrates.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) was first described in 1980 in six newborns.
adaptation2.2: It is caused by a single gene that is involved in development of multiple body parts. The problems include a non-cancer mass in the lower part of the brain and extra fingers and toes, among others.
adaptation2.3: This disorder is passed down by either parent, and the involved gene is located on chromosome 7, associating PHS with the gene called GLI3.
adaptation2.4: Variants of the the GLI3 gene in which some genetic information is missing or misplaced are associated with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome (GCPS) that affects development of the hands, feet, head, and face.
adaptation2.5: Patients with both PHS and GCPS have extra or merged fingers and toes, and abnormal heads and faces. Both PHS and GCPS are passed down from either parent, but the clinical signs of these diseases are different.
adaptation2.6: The additional finger in GCPS is usually located next to the thumb. In PHS, the extra finger is in the center or next to the little finger (pinky). The extra toes follow the same pattern: in GCPS the sixth toe is next to the big toe.
adaptation2.7: No reported cases of GCPS have non-cancer growth in the lower part of the brain, and PHS does not cause increased distance between the eyes or broadening of the nose or forehead.
adaptation2.8: Because the generic changes for PHS and GCPS share the location on the chromosome, we study GLI3 as a gene potentially responsible for PHS.
adaptation2.9: We describe two PHS families with large changes in the GLI3 gene. In one family the change is new and there is no family history of PHS.
adaptation2.10: The data show that changes in the GLI3 gene, which are passed down in the family or happen for the first time, cause PHS. Large-scale  changes in the GLI3 gene can change the development of  many tissues and organs.

15617553.Title: Psychiatric and neuropsychological characterization of Pallister-Hall syndrome

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare, single-gene, malformation syndrome that includes central polydactyly, hypothalamic hamartoma, bifid epiglottis, endocrine dysfunction, and other anomalies.
abstract.2: The syndrome has variable clinical manifestations and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
abstract.3: We sought to determine whether psychiatric disorders and/or neuropsychological impairment were characteristic of PHS.
abstract.4: We prospectively conducted systematic neuropsychiatric evaluations with 19 PHS subjects ranging in age from 7 to 75 years.
abstract.5: The evaluation included detailed clinical interviews, clinician-rated and self-report instruments, and a battery of neuropsychological tests.
abstract.6: Seven of 14 adult PHS subjects met diagnostic criteria for at least one DSM-IV Axis I disorder.
abstract.7: Three additional subjects demonstrated developmental delays and/or neuropsychological deficits on formal neuropsychological testing.
abstract.8: However, we found no characteristic psychiatric phenotype associated with PHS, and the frequency of each of the diagnoses observed in these subjects was not different from that expected in this size sample.
abstract.9: The overall frequency of psychiatric findings among all patients with PHS cannot be compared to point prevalence estimates of psychiatric disease in the general population because of biased ascertainment.
abstract.10: This limitation is inherent to the study of behavioral phenotypes in rare disorders.
abstract.11: The general issue of psychiatric evaluation of rare genetic syndromes is discussed in light of this negative result.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare disease caused by changes in a single gene (the basic unit of inheritance.) The abnormalities include extra fingers and toes, growth of non-cancer masses in the brain, changes in the flap that protect the windpipe, improper function of the endocrine system that regulates body functions through hormones, and other problems.
adaptation2.2: The signs of this disease vary and are passed down through either parent.
adaptation2.3: We studied if PHS causes any mental health problems.
adaptation2.4: We measured how well the brain is working in 19 PHS patients ranging in age from 7 to 75 years.

abstract.1: Clinical characteristics: Pallister-Hall syndrome (referred to as PHS in this entry) is characterized by a spectrum of anomalies ranging from polydactyly, asymptomatic bifid epiglottis, and hypothalamic hamartoma at the mild end to laryngotracheal cleft with neonatal lethality at the severe end.
abstract.2: Individuals with mild PHS may be incorrectly diagnosed as having isolated postaxial polydactyly type A.
abstract.3: Individuals with PHS can have pituitary insufficiency and may die as neonates from undiagnosed and untreated adrenal insufficiency.
abstract.4: Diagnosis/testing: The diagnosis of Pallister-Hall syndrome can be established in a proband with both hypothalamic hamartoma and mesoaxial polydactyly.
abstract.5: Identification of a heterozygous pathogenic variant in GLI3 confirms the diagnosis.
abstract.6: Management: Treatment of manifestations: Urgent treatment for endocrine abnormalities, especially cortisol deficiency; management of epiglottic abnormalities depending on the abnormality and the extent of respiratory compromise.
abstract.7: Bifid epiglottis, the most common abnormality, typically does not need treatment.
abstract.8: Standard treatment of anal atresia or stenosis; symptomatic treatment of seizures; elective repair of polydactyly; developmental intervention or special education for developmental delays.
abstract.9: Prevention of secondary complications: Biopsy or resection of hypothalamic hamartoma may result in complications and lifelong need for hormone replacement; seizures may begin or worsen with use of stimulants for attention deficit disorder.
abstract.10: Surveillance: During childhood, annual developmental assessment and annual medical evaluation to assess growth and monitor for signs of precocious puberty.
abstract.11: Genetic counseling: Pallister-Hall syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
abstract.12: Individuals with PHS may have an affected parent or may have the disorder as the result of a de novo pathogenic variant.
abstract.13: About 25% of individuals have a de novo pathogenic variant.
abstract.14: Persons with a de novo pathogenic variant are generally more severely affected than those with a family history of PHS.
abstract.15: The risk to offspring of an affected individual is 50%.
abstract.16: Prenatal testing for pregnancies at increased risk is possible if the pathogenic variant in the family is known.
abstract.17: The reliability of ultrasound examination for prenatal diagnosis is unknown.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) ranges from mild to severe cases. Mild cases include polydactyly, in which people have six fingers or toes,  a harmless split in the epiglottis (a small leaf-shaped structure that prevents food and drink from entering the windpipe) and hypothalamic hamartoma, a noncancerous growth in the base of the brain that can cause seizures and other problems. The severe cases include laryngotracheal cleft, a defect in which the baby's airway and food passages are connected, which can lead to newborn's death if the food and saliva get into the lungs.
adaptation2.2: Mild PHS might be confused with babies having one or more extra finger or toe at birth, called postaxial polydactyly type A.
adaptation2.3: In people with PHS pituitary gland, located in the brain, might not produce enough hormones (substances that regulate growth, metabolism and other functions). People with PHS may have adrenal insufficiency, a condition in which the adrenal glands do not produce enough hormones to control blood pressure, metabolism and the immune system. If these conditions are not recognized and treated in newborns, they may die.
adaptation2.4: Hypothalamic hamartoma (non-cancer growth in the brain) and extra fingers or toes may be caused by Pallister-Hall syndrome.
adaptation2.5: Genetic testing confirms the patients have PHS.
adaptation2.6: Urgent treatments are needed if the glands do not produce enough hormones, especially cortisol. The defect in the flap that covers the windpipe needs treatment if it can lead to problems with breathing.
adaptation2.7: Bifid epiglottis, the split in the flap that covers the windpipe, typically does not need treatment.
adaptation2.8: Standard treatments are used for problems with anus, such as narrowing of the anal canal. Patients can choose to repair extra fingers. Seizures are treated as needed. Special education and other support are provided for developmental delays.
adaptation2.9: Treatments of the problems caused by PHS can have complications. After surgery for the hypothalamic hamartoma patients may need to take hormones for the rest of their life. Drugs for attention deficit disorder may cause or worsen seizures.
adaptation2.10: Every year, children with PHS need evaluation of their mental development, growth, and signs of their body changing into that of an adult (puberty) too soon.
adaptation2.11: Either parent passes down the disease.
adaptation2.12: A child will have PHS if either parent passes down the disease or if a new variant develops before birth.
adaptation2.13: About a quarter of the PHS patients have a new harmful variant.
adaptation2.14: Persons with a new harmful variant have a more severe disease than those with a family history of PHS.
adaptation2.15: Chances of getting or not getting the disease from the parent  are equal.
adaptation2.16: If the harmful variant runs in the family, the developing baby may be tested during pregnancy.
adaptation2.17: It is not known if ultrasound during pregnancy will show PHS.

26604140.Title: Urogenital development in Pallister-Hall syndrome is disrupted in a cell-lineage-specific manner by constitutive expression of GLI3 repressor

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare disorder caused by mutations in GLI3 that produce a transcriptional repressor (GLI3R).
abstract.2: Individuals with PHS present with a variably penetrant variety of urogenital system malformations, including renal aplasia or hypoplasia, hydroureter, hydronephrosis or a common urogenital sinus.
abstract.3: The embryologic mechanisms controlled by GLI3R that result in these pathologic phenotypes are undefined.
abstract.4: We demonstrate that germline expression of GLI3R causes renal hypoplasia, associated with decreased nephron number, and hydroureter and hydronephrosis, caused by blind-ending ureters.
abstract.5: Mice with obligate GLI3R expression also displayed duplication of the ureters that was caused by aberrant common nephric duct patterning and ureteric stalk outgrowth.
abstract.6: These developmental abnormalities are associated with suppressed Hedgehog signaling activity in the cloaca and adjacent vesicular mesenchyme.
abstract.7: Mice with conditional expression of GLI3R were utilized to identify lineage-specific effects of GLI3R.
abstract.8: In the ureteric bud, GLI3R expression decreased branching morphogenesis.
abstract.9: In Six2-positive nephrogenic progenitors, GLI3R decreased progenitor cell proliferation reducing the number of nephrogenic precursor structures.
abstract.10: Using mutant mice with Gli3R and Gli3 null alleles, we demonstrate that urogenital system patterning and development is controlled by the levels of GLI3R and not by an absence of full-length GLI3.
abstract.11: We conclude that the urogenital system phenotypes observed in PHS are caused by GLI3R-dependent perturbations in nephric duct patterning, renal branching morphogenesis and nephrogenic progenitor self-renewal.

adaptation2.4: We show that variations in the GLI3 gene cause poor development of the kidneys, and a closed end in the duct that runs between the kidney and the bladder, which causes swelling of the kidneys and the duct.

adaptation2.6: The abnormal development is caused by the lack of information the embryonic cells (cells that forms when eggs are fertilized)  need for proper development.
adaptation2.10: Using mutant mice, we show that the development of the reproduction and urinary organs  is controlled by the variants in the GLI3 gene.
adaptation2.11: Different problems in PHS are caused by the different mistakes in the development of the urinary organs due to the information provided by the variants of the GLI3 gene.

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is an extremely rare syndrome of unknown prevalence with autosomal dominant inheritance due to GLI3 gene mutations classically characterized by the presence of a hypothalamic hamartoma and polydactyly.

17679728.Title: A phase II placebo-controlled trial of neoadjuvant anastrozole alone or with gefitinib in early breast cancer

abstract.1: Purpose: Increased epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) expression may promote breast cancer resistance to endocrine therapy.
abstract.2: We have therefore investigated whether neoadjuvant gefitinib, an EGFR inhibitor, might overcome biologic and clinical resistance to neoadjuvant anastrozole in a phase II placebo-controlled trial.
abstract.3: Patients and methods: Postmenopausal women with stage I to IIIB hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer received anastrozole 1 mg daily for 16 weeks and were randomly assigned at a ratio of 2:5:5 to receive, in addition, gefitinib 250 mg/d orally for 16 weeks: placebo 1 tablet/d orally for 2 weeks and then gefitinib for 14 weeks or placebo for 16 weeks.
abstract.4: The primary end point was biologic change in proliferation as measured by Ki67 at 2 and 16 weeks; the main secondary end point was overall objective response (OR).
abstract.5: Results: Two hundred six women were randomly assigned.
abstract.6: Mean changes in Ki67 with anastrozole and gefitinib versus anastrozole alone were -77.4% and -83.6%, respectively, between baseline and 16 weeks (geometric mean ratio = 1.37; 95% CI, 0.79 to 2.39; P = .26), -80.1% and -71.3% between baseline and 2 weeks (geometric mean ratio = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.39 to 1.25; P = .22) and -19.3% and -43% (geometric mean ratio = 1.42; 95% CI, 0.86 to 2.35; P = .16) between 2 and 16 weeks.
abstract.7: ORs in the combination and anastrozole alone groups were 48% and 61% (estimated difference = -13.1%; 95% CI, -27.3% to 1.2%), respectively, with a nonsignificant trend against the combination (P = .08) and 48% versus 72% (estimated difference = -24.1%; 95% CI, -45.3% to -2.9%) in the progesterone-receptor-positive subgroup, which was significant (P = .03) and consistent with Ki67 changes.
abstract.8: Common treatment-related adverse events included diarrhea, rash, alopecia, dry skin, and nausea.
abstract.9: There was no evidence of a pharmacokinetic interaction.
abstract.10: Conclusion: Addition of gefitinib to neoadjuvant anastrozole had no additional clinical or biologic effect, failing to support our original hypothesis.

20821047.Title: Anastrozole and letrozole: an investigation and comparison of quality of life and tolerability

abstract.1: Previous studies have demonstrated that both anastrozole and letrozole are well tolerated.
abstract.2: Letrozole suppresses estrogen to a greater degree than anastrozole in the serum and breast tumor.
abstract.3: Concerns have been raised that greater potency may adversely affect patients' quality of life (QOL).
abstract.4: One hundred eighty-one postmenopausal women with invasive estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers were randomized to receive either 12 weeks of letrozole followed by 12 weeks of anastrozole or the reverse sequence.
abstract.5: One hundred and six received immediate adjuvant aromatase inhibitors (AIs) following surgery, and 75 received extended adjuvant therapy.
abstract.6: The Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy Endocrine Subscale (FACT-B-ES) QOL questionnaires were completed to assess QOL on each drug.
abstract.7: Additional side-effect profiles were collected.
abstract.8: Each patient completed a patient preference form.
abstract.9: Twenty-one patients withdrew before study end, 10/179 (5.6%) while taking letrozole and 4/173 (2.3%) while taking anastrozole (P = 0.12).
abstract.10: Tamoxifen-naïve patients had a higher mean ES (endocrine symptoms subscale) score at entry versus those having extended therapy (66.0 vs. 61.9; P = 0.001).
abstract.11: There was no significant change in FACT-B-ES (overall) scores or ES scores while patients were taking anastrozole or letrozole and no significant differences between drugs.
abstract.12: Nearly 80% of patients reported one or more side effects with either agent.
abstract.13: No differences in frequency, grade, or range of side effects were seen between drugs.
abstract.14: Of 160 patients, 49 (30.6%) preferred letrozole, 57 (35.6%) preferred anastrozole, and 54 (33.8%) had no preference (P = 0.26, Pearson's Chi-squared test).
abstract.15: In conclusion, both AIs are equally well tolerated.
abstract.16: There were no significant differences in QOL scores between the two drugs.

24037977.Title: Alopecia with endocrine therapies in patients with cancer

abstract.1: Background: Whereas the frequency of alopecia to cytotoxic chemotherapies has been well described, the incidence of alopecia during endocrine therapies (i.e., anti-estrogens, aromatase inhibitors) has not been investigated.
abstract.2: Endocrine agents are widely used in the treatment and prevention of many solid tumors, principally those of the breast and prostate.
abstract.3: Adherence to these therapies is suboptimal, in part because of toxicities.
abstract.4: We performed a systematic analysis of the literature to ascertain the incidence and risk for alopecia in patients receiving endocrine therapies.
abstract.5: Results: Data from 19,430 patients in 35 clinical trials were available for analysis.
abstract.6: Of these, 13,415 patients had received endocrine treatments and 6,015 patients served as controls.
abstract.7: The incidence of all-grade alopecia ranged from 0% to 25%, with an overall incidence of 4.4% (95% confidence interval: 3.3%-5.9%).

24197658.Title: Aromatase inhibitor therapy and hair loss among breast cancer survivors

abstract.1: The objective of this study was to examine the associations between aromatase inhibitor therapy and hair loss or hair thinning among female breast cancer survivors.
abstract.2: Data were analyzed from 851 female breast cancer survivors who responded to a hospital registry-based survey.
abstract.3: Data on hair loss, hair thinning, demographic characteristics, and health habits were based on self-report; data on aromatase inhibitor therapy were collected on the survey and verified using medical record review.
abstract.4: Logistic regression was used to estimate the odds ratios (ORs) and 95 % confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations between aromatase inhibitor therapy and the hair outcome variables adjusted for potential confounders, including age and chemotherapy treatment.
abstract.5: The results showed that 22.4 % of the breast cancer survivors reported hair loss and 31.8 % reported hair thinning.
abstract.6: In the confounder-adjusted analyses, breast cancer survivors who were within 2 years of starting aromatase inhibitor treatment at the time of survey completion were approximately two and a half times more likely to report reporting hair loss (OR 2.55; 95 % CI 1.19-5.45) or hair thinning (OR 2.33; 95 % CI 1.10-4.93) within the past 4 weeks compared to those who were never treated with an aromatase inhibitor.
abstract.7: Current aromatase inhibitor use for two or more years at the time of the survey and prior use were significantly associated with hair thinning (current users, ≥2 years: OR 1.86; prior users: OR 1.62), but not hair loss.
abstract.8: Findings from this study suggest that aromatase inhibitor use is associated with an increased risk of hair loss and hair thinning independent of chemotherapy and age; these side effects are likely due to the substantial decrease in estrogen concentrations resulting from treatment with this drug.
abstract.9: Future research should focus on examining these associations in a prospective manner using more detailed and objective measures of hair loss and thinning.

abstract.4: All of the adjuvant hormonal anticancer drugs that were used in the patients are antiestrogenic agents, either aromatase inhibitors or selective estrogen receptor modulators.

26108239.Title: Adjuvant aromatase inhibitor therapy in early breast cancer: what factors lead patients to discontinue treatment?

abstract.1: Background: Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are standard hormone therapy (HT) for the adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal endocrine-sensitive early breast cancer.
abstract.2: Treatment discontinuation due to toxicity is an important issue that may help clinicians identify effective clinical interventions to allow adequate treatment duration.
abstract.3: We reviewed the main reasons for interruption of AIs at our institution from 2006 to 2009.
abstract.4: Methods: 236 patients treated with adjuvant AIs were eligible for analysis.
abstract.5: Median age was 64 years (35-89), median follow-up 53 months (6-60).
abstract.6: Prior adjuvant chemotherapy was taxane based in 47 patients and anthracycline based in 43 patients.
abstract.7: 118 patients had received letrozole, 101 anastrozole, and 17 exemestane.
abstract.8: Results: Twenty-four patients (10%) needed discontinuation of the first AI assigned as a result of toxicity.
abstract.9: Grade 2/3 arthralgia was the main reason for discontinuation in 13/24 patients.
abstract.10: No differences in the incidence of arthralgia were noted in patients who had received taxanes or anthracyclines.
abstract.11: Headache, alopecia, itching, diffuse skin reaction, allergic reaction with hypertensive crisis, xerostomia and xerophthalmia, insomnia and somnolence were the other reasons for discontinuation.
abstract.12: In multivariate logistic regression analysis, age (65 years) and HT were independent factors associated with the onset of arthralgia (p = 0.006 and p = 0.008, respectively; OR 2.65, 95% CI 1.32-5.31).
abstract.13: Alternative HT (AI or tamoxifen) was offered to patients who wanted or needed to permanently interrupt the ongoing drug.
abstract.14: Conclusions: In our analysis, 10% of patients discontinued the first AI assigned because of toxicity.
abstract.15: Median time course of all adverse events leading to HT discontinuation was 155 days and 135 days for arthralgia.
abstract.16: A switch to alternative HT with toxicity monitoring is a recommended option for avoiding premature and permanent interruption of an effective treatment.
